extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and writers in English (playwrights and versifiers)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing English poetry and drama (tragedy, comedy, pastoral, and versification), emphasizing unity, diction, appropriate use of comic elements, and the strengths of the English tongue. Drawn from an Elizabethan-era defence of poesy addressed to practicing poets/playwrights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy bound to the laws of poesy, not history
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is tied to the laws of poesy, and not of history; it is not bound to follow historical sequence but has liberty to feign new matter or frame the history to the most tragical convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not slavishly reproduce historical chronology. The poet may compress, omit, or rearrange events to bring out the principal tragic action and heighten effect. Example: rather than beginning at the delivery of Polydorus, Euripides begins with the finding of the body and leaves prior events to narration. Emphasize tragic unity and convenience over literal historical completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid representing many places on stage (unity of place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays should not gratuitously attempt to represent many distinct places in one performance; frequent shifts of setting are absurd for the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes that imply Asia, Africa, caves, rocks, shipwrecks, pitched fields, etc., strain audience credulity when the stage is required to do them all in quick succession. If the story requires distant places, use reported narration (nuntius) rather than attempting to enact every locale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive time-compression (unity of time) and unnecessary longue durée
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not compress many years and life-events into the brief time of a play in ways that strain sense; tragedies should keep to a credible temporal scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes examples where multiple generations, births, losses, coming-to-age, courtship and second pregnancies are all implied within 'two hours'. Use the conventions of poesy to shape time credibly. Example: Terence's Eunuch was fit for its time-frame; other plays that pretend many years within a short performance are absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin at the principal point (avoid beginning 'ab ovo')
rubrics_metrics.description: As Horace advises, a writer must not 'begin ab ovo' (from the egg/origin) but must come to the principal point of the one action to be represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the decisive moment or scene which most serve the tragic or comic purpose and open there rather than attempting to present the whole backstory. Example: begin with the discovery of Polydorus's body rather than his delivery in childhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narration for things that cannot be represented
rubrics_metrics.description: Many matters that are easily recounted cannot be shown onstage and should therefore be reported by a messenger or narrator rather than mime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts speech (reporting, as of distant Peru or Calicut) with action (representation) and notes classical practice of using a 'Nuntius' to recount events done elsewhere or in former time. Use this device to preserve plausibility when an event is impractical to stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain genre and tonal propriety (avoid mongrel tragi-comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mix kings and clowns without cause: do not thrust comic clowns into majestical, tragic matters by force. Tragi-comedy should be rare and tasteful; mixing without decency spoils both genres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid injections of low buffoonery into weighty scenes; the result is neither proper tragedy nor proper comedy. Ancient examples of tragi-comedy are rare and delicate; the modern practice of mismatching 'horn-pipes and funerals' produces scurrility instead of the admiration or delight each genre should produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should aim at delight and teaching, not mere scornful laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the comical part should not rest on scornful matters that stir laughter only; comedy should mix laughter with that 'delightful teaching' which is the end of poesy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish delight (a positive, often permanent pleasure) from mere laughter (often scornful and transient). Good comedy produces both where appropriate but grounds its laughter in human foibles that instruct rather than in cruelty or execrable subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make laughter from sinful or pitiable things (ethical limits of mockery)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is forbidden plainly by Aristotle to stir laughter at sinful or miserable things which are rather to be execrated or pitied than mocked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make the audience gape at wretched poverty or jeer at strangers (e.g., mocking language deficiencies). Better comic targets are vanity, hypocrisy, self-conceit — characters whose ridicule can produce teaching and wholesome delight (examples: a busy loving courtier, a self-wise schoolmaster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: prefer naturalness; avoid far-fetched, affected words and ostentatious figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The outward manner (diction) is often worse than the matter: writers use far-fetched words, exotic diction, and over-elaborate figures, producing affectation instead of natural speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'honey-flowing matron eloquence' and forcing obscure or strange words on an English audience. Imitate great orators by assimilating their effects rather than slavishly importing their phrases or 'devouring them whole' from manuals of figures. The aim is to 'hide art'—use art to persuade, not to show off cleverness. Preachers and scholars are warned against this excess as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use similitudes (similes) sparingly and for explanation, not ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Similitudes are for explaining to a willing hearer; their force is not to prove a point to an opponent. Excessive or crowded similitudes merely weary the ear and distract the memory from the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pillaging lists of animal and herb similes to ornament every conceit. Once the similitude has performed its explanatory function, further elaboration is tedious and unhelpful. Favor apt, concise comparisons over multitudes of strained images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural persuasion (popular ear) to learned ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers who win popular credence (e.g. Antonius and Crassus) did not rely on visible art; a plain sensibleness often persuades more than elaborate rhetorical display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courtier's practice (what fits nature) often achieves true rhetorical art without self-conscious display; avoid bringing in art merely to show art. The end of eloquence is persuasion; aim for clarity and force rather than curious speech that pleases the eye but persuades few.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose versification to suit English strengths (accent, caesura, rhyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: English is well-suited both to ancient quantity-based versification and to modern accent-and-rhyme-based verse; English has advantages (strong accent, caesura, variety of masculine/feminine/antepenultimate rhymes) other vernaculars lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether using ancient quantity or modern rhyme, exploit what English naturally allows: precise accentual patterns, cæsura (breathing-place), and a variety of rhyme types (masculine, feminine, sdrucciola). Use the form that best serves musicality and the expression of passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind both matter and manner: employ subject and diction rightly
rubrics_metrics.description: Poesy requires right use of matter (subject) and manner (diction); both are essential to true poetic art and to the honour of the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to the substantive point of poesy (material) as well as to the outward words (manner). Cure the 'common infection' among writers by acknowledging faults in both matter and manner and bending toward a natural, effective use of language.
